lessonInput.title: Objects and classes
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance. Claim 1: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. Claim 2: Individual objects created from a class are called instances. Claim 3: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

claims: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

anchors.quote: In a Python program, a class defines a type of object with attributes (fields) and methods (procedures)
A class is a blueprint for creating objects
Individual objects created of the class type are called instances
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class defines a type of object and serves as its blueprint.
keyTerms.eg: A class is used as the blueprint for creating objects.
keyTerms.mi: A class is an individual object created from a blueprint.
keyTerms.cx: The created individual is an instance; the class supplies the blueprint.

keyTerms.df: Objects are entities built from a class, with each one called an instance.
keyTerms.eg: Objects created from a class are individual instances.
keyTerms.mi: Objects define the methods shared by every instance.
keyTerms.cx: The class defines the shared methods, while objects are built from that class.

keyTerms.df: Instances are individual objects whose attributes are carried as their own copies.
keyTerms.eg: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes.
keyTerms.mi: Instances define the methods that the class shares.
keyTerms.cx: Methods come from the class and are shared by its instances.

scenario.su: Students must classify a class and two objects as either a blueprint or instances before a deadline. They must also distinguish the separate attribute copies from the methods shared by both objects.
scenario.ma: class passage stating that it is a blueprint for creating objects, object passages identifying two individual objects created from the class, attribute observation showing each instance carrying its own copy, method observation showing class-defined methods shared by both instances

mc.q: An object is observed being built from a class, and the task is to label the class and the built object. Which comparison uses the source terms correctly?
op: Class is method; built object is class
Class is attribute; built object is blueprint
Class is blueprint; built object is instance
Class is instance; built object is method
mc.ex: The class serves as the blueprint, and an object built from it is an instance. Describing the class as an instance confuses the blueprint with the individual object built from it.

mc.q: Two objects have separate attribute copies and use methods defined by their class. Which account correctly connects the observed objects, attributes, methods, and class?
op: Instances define attribute copies and carry class methods
Instances create class methods and share blueprints
Instances share attribute copies and define class methods
Instances carry attribute copies and share class methods
mc.ex: Each instance carries its own attribute copy, while methods defined by the class are shared by the instances. Saying instances share attribute copies and define class methods reverses both stated relationships.

facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
keyTerms.eg: A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
keyTerms.mi: A class is only a set of instructions for creating objects.
keyTerms.cx: A class is a blueprint for creating objects because it defines a type of object with attributes and methods.

keyTerms.df: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
keyTerms.eg: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
keyTerms.mi: Instances are the blueprints used to construct new classes.
keyTerms.cx: Individual objects created from a class are called instances because they are the actual objects built from the blueprint.

keyTerms.df: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
keyTerms.eg: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
keyTerms.mi: Methods are unique to each instance and not shared across objects.
keyTerms.cx: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance because they are defined by the class blueprint.

scenario.su: A developer needs to create a system for managing different types of vehicles, requiring a structure that defines common properties and actions. The constraint is that the system must allow multiple distinct vehicle records to exist simultaneously, each with unique identification numbers.
scenario.ma: Compare the structure of a class definition for a 'Car' versus an instance of that class, noting how attributes and methods are handled.

mc.q: When a class is used as a blueprint, what is the resulting entity that is built from it?
op: The blueprint itself
The class definition
An object instance
The set of methods
mc.ex: Individual objects created from a class are called instances, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

mc.q: If a class defines attributes and methods, how are the methods related across different objects created from that class?
op: Each instance carries its own copy
Methods are unique to each instance
Methods are shared by every instance
Methods are defined only by the blueprint
mc.ex: The methods defined by the class are shared by every instance, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

lessonInput.title: User scenarios
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A user scenario is a narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction. Claim 1: Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user. Claim 2: A scenario should state who the user is, why and where they act, what goal they have, and how they pursue it. Claim 3: Scenario work can reveal how needs vary with context and across diverse users. Claim 4: Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.

claims: A user scenario is a narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
A scenario should state who the user is, why and where they act, what goal they have, and how they pursue it.
Scenario work can reveal how needs vary with context and across diverse users.
Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.

anchors.quote: tells a story about how users interact
specific interaction for a specific user
Who they are
needs might vary depending on their context
validation, feedback, and refinement

facts: A user scenario is a narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
A scenario should state who the user is, why and where they act, what goal they have, and how they pursue it.
Scenario work can reveal how needs vary with context and across diverse users.
Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.

keyTerms.df: A user scenario is a narrative distinguished by situating specified user elements within a specific interaction.
keyTerms.eg: A team writes who the user is, why and where they act, their goal, and how they pursue it.
keyTerms.mi: A user scenario communicates a design idea without situating a user type or context.
keyTerms.cx: The narrative must place the user type and context within the interaction, so those elements cannot be omitted.

keyTerms.df: A specific interaction is the setting through which scenarios communicate a design idea for a specific user.
keyTerms.eg: A scenario connects a specific user, goal, and tasks within the interaction.
keyTerms.mi: A specific interaction replaces the need to identify who acts and what goal they have.
keyTerms.cx: The interaction does not replace those details; the scenario should state the user and goal as well.

keyTerms.df: The represented user group is a participant in the validation and refinement of scenarios alongside collaborators.
keyTerms.eg: Teams ask the represented user group and collaborators to validate and refine a scenario.
keyTerms.mi: Collaborators should refine scenarios before the represented user group validates them separately.
keyTerms.cx: Both the represented users and collaborators belong in validation and refinement, rather than being assigned separate roles.

scenario.su: A team must classify a user scenario as stating or omitting the contents a scenario should state. Its decision is constrained to a narrative passage that states who the user is and why and where they act, plus a tasks notation that omits the goal and how the user pursues it.
scenario.ma: narrative passage stating who the user is and why and where they act; tasks notation omitting the goal and how the user pursues it

mc.q: A reviewer compares a narrative that situates user elements with scenarios that present a design idea; which distinction correctly describes the narrative and the specific interaction?
op: Narratives situate design ideas; scenarios communicate user types
Narratives communicate users; scenarios situate design ideas
Narratives situate elements; scenarios communicate design ideas
Narratives communicate contexts; scenarios situate specific users
mc.ex: A user-scenario narrative situates the user elements, while scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction. Assigning the design idea to what the narrative situates swaps these relationships.

mc.q: A team compares scenario drafts before review: one records who, why, where, the goal, and its pursuit, while the others omit a recorded element. Which draft should it select?
op: Choose why, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, why, where, and goal
Choose who, why, where, goal, and pursuit
mc.ex: A scenario should state who acts, why and where they act, their goal, and how they pursue it. Stopping at the goal omits how the user pursues it.

facts: A user scenario is a narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
A scenario should state who the user is, why and where they act, what goal they have, and how they pursue it.
Scenario work can reveal how needs vary with context and across diverse users.
Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.

keyTerms.df: A narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
keyTerms.eg: A narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
keyTerms.mi: A user scenario is just a simple description of a user's actions without detailing the motivation or context.
keyTerms.cx: A user scenario must include the user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.

keyTerms.df: Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
keyTerms.eg: A narrative that communicates a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
keyTerms.mi: Communicating a design idea means simply describing the final interface without showing the interaction.
keyTerms.cx: Communicating a design idea requires showing how a design idea is communicated through a specific interaction for a specific user.

keyTerms.df: Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.
keyTerms.eg: Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.
keyTerms.mi: Validating scenarios means checking if the narrative is grammatically correct and easy to read.
keyTerms.cx: Validating scenarios means checking if the narrative is validated with the represented user group and collaborators.

scenario.su: A user is a senior citizen trying to access a government service online, motivated by the need for accessibility, in a public library setting, with the goal of successfully completing a complex form. The constraint is that the user has limited digital literacy and only has access to a public computer.
scenario.ma: User type: Senior citizen. Motivation: Need for accessibility. Context: Public library setting. Goal: Successfully completing a complex form. Constraint: Limited digital literacy and public computer access.

mc.q: When communicating a design idea, what is the primary function of a user scenario according to the supplied claims?
op: It shows a visual mockup of a screen.
It communicates a design idea through a specific interaction.
It details the general needs of a user type.
It lists all possible user tasks in sequence.
mc.ex: Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user, while showing a visual mockup of a screen is not the primary function.

mc.q: Given the need to reveal how needs vary, what action should teams take regarding user scenarios?
op: They should only create scenarios for the primary user.
They should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group.
They should ignore context when refining the narrative.
They should focus only on the user's stated goal.
mc.ex: Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators, while ignoring context when refining the narrative is incorrect.

lessonInput.title: Dictionaries
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position. Claim 1: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys. Claim 2: Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

claims: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

anchors.quote: A dictionary in Python is a container object including key-value pairs
a dictionary object cannot hold duplicate key values

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

facts: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

keyTerms.df: A dictionary is a structure that stores key-value pairs and looks up values using keys.
keyTerms.eg: A Python dictionary is written with curly braces in key: value form.
keyTerms.mi: A dictionary looks up each key by its value.
keyTerms.cx: Dictionary lookup uses a key to find its associated value.

keyTerms.df: Key-value pairs associate stored values with keys used to look up those values.
keyTerms.eg: Dictionaries store key-value pairs for naturally labeled data.
keyTerms.mi: Key-value pairs require values to be found by numeric position.
keyTerms.cx: Values in key-value pairs are found using their associated keys.

keyTerms.df: Curly braces are the notation used to write dictionaries in key: value form.
keyTerms.eg: Dictionaries use curly braces around key: value form.
keyTerms.mi: Curly braces show that data is naturally ordered.
keyTerms.cx: Naturally labeled data makes dictionaries ideal, while curly braces provide their written form.

scenario.su: A dictionary is written with curly braces in key: value form, and the data is naturally labeled rather than ordered. Decide whether lookup uses a key or a numeric position, under the constraint that the dictionary cannot hold duplicate keys.
scenario.ma: curly braces in key: value form observation, naturally labeled rather than ordered data observation, lookup-by-key design

mc.q: A dictionary stores key-value pairs, and an observation contrasts lookup by a key with lookup by a numeric position; which proposition captures the supported distinction?
op: Keys are looked up using values
Numeric positions are looked up using values
Values are looked up using numeric positions
Values are looked up using keys
mc.ex: A dictionary finds each value using its associated key rather than a numeric position. Looking up keys using values reverses the stated relationship.

mc.q: A Python design uses curly braces in key: value form but presents duplicate keys; under a deadline, how should students classify it while respecting both observed details?
op: It is ideal for naturally ordered data
It is a dictionary with duplicate keys
It looks up keys by each value
It cannot be a dictionary as presented
mc.ex: A dictionary cannot hold duplicate keys because it looks up values using keys. Curly-brace key: value form does not make duplicate keys compatible with a dictionary.

facts: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

keyTerms.df: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
keyTerms.eg: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
keyTerms.mi: A dictionary stores data in a sequence where the position determines the retrieval method.
keyTerms.cx: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.

keyTerms.df: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
keyTerms.eg: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
keyTerms.mi: A key in a dictionary can be repeated multiple times to store different values.
keyTerms.cx: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.

keyTerms.df: Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.
keyTerms.eg: Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.
keyTerms.mi: Curly braces are only used for defining function parameters in Python code.
keyTerms.cx: Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

scenario.su: A data structure is being used to store user preferences for a system, and the system requires fast retrieval based on a specific user ID. The developer must decide how to structure the data to ensure unique identification for each user profile.
scenario.ma: Compare the structure {'user_id': 101, 'name': 'Alice'} and {'user_id': 101, 'name': 'Bob'} to determine which structure is valid for the system's requirements.

mc.q: Which characteristic distinguishes a dictionary from a structure that relies on numeric position for data retrieval?
op: A structure uses numeric position for retrieval.
A structure stores data in key-value pairs.
A structure cannot hold duplicate keys.
A structure is ideal for ordered data.
mc.ex: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

mc.q: Given the constraint that a dictionary cannot hold duplicate keys, which data structure is appropriate for storing unique user IDs?
op: A list where IDs can be repeated.
A dictionary using user IDs as keys.
A tuple with unique numeric indices.
A sequence ordered by numeric position.
mc.ex: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys, which is the subject evidence supporting the answer, then correct the closest distractor.

lessonInput.title: Conditionals and boolean logic
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions. Claim 1: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false. Claim 2: An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false. Claim 3: and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.
lessonInput.readings: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

claims: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

anchors.quote: When an if-else statement is executed, one and only one of the branches is taken
If the condition is true, the body is executed. If the condition is false, the body is not executed
An else statement is used with an if statement and contains a body of statements that is executed when the if statement's condition is false
The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

facts: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

keyTerms.df: A conditional statement selects a block according to whether its condition is true.
keyTerms.eg: When a condition is true, the conditional statement chooses which block runs.
keyTerms.mi: A conditional statement requires boolean operators to choose a block.
keyTerms.cx: Block selection can be based on whether a condition is true; a compound condition is not required.

keyTerms.df: An if statement is a conditional form whose body runs when its condition is true.
keyTerms.eg: When the if condition is false, the if statement skips its body.
keyTerms.mi: An if statement runs its body when its condition is false.
keyTerms.cx: A false condition leads the body to be skipped, not run.

keyTerms.df: An else clause contains statements associated with a false if condition.
keyTerms.eg: If the condition is false, the statements in the else clause run.
keyTerms.mi: An else clause holds statements for a true if condition.
keyTerms.cx: Its statements correspond to the condition being false rather than true.

scenario.su: A student must label which block runs in an if-else before a deadline, with the recorded if condition marked false. The student must also distinguish a compound condition recorded as true or false, using the noted and, or, and not operators.
scenario.ma: if condition notation marked false, if-body observation marked skipped, else-clause observation marked run, and-or-not condition table marked true or false

mc.q: An if condition is observed as false, and its else clause holds statements. Which result correctly identifies the if body and the else statements?
op: Running if body; skipped else statements
Skipped if body; skipped else statements
Running if body; running else statements
Skipped if body; running else statements
mc.ex: A false if condition makes the if statement skip its body, and the else clause holds statements that run for that false condition. A running if body with skipped else statements reverses those results.

mc.q: A compound condition records one condition as true and the other as false; students must classify both results before a deadline. Which notation correctly compares and with or?
op: and and or are both False
and and or are both True
and is False; or is True
and is True; or is False
mc.ex: and returns True only when both conditions are true, while or returns True when either condition is true. They therefore do not both return True for these recorded conditions.

facts: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

keyTerms.df: A conditional statement selects which code block executes based on a condition's truth value.
keyTerms.eg: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true.
keyTerms.mi: A conditional statement executes multiple code blocks depending on the condition's truth value.
keyTerms.cx: A conditional statement takes exactly one branch, meaning it chooses only one path based on the condition's truth value.

keyTerms.df: An if statement executes its body only when the specified condition evaluates to true.
keyTerms.eg: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true.
keyTerms.mi: An if statement executes its body when the condition is false and skips it when true.
keyTerms.cx: An if statement skips its body when the condition is false, executing it only when the condition is true.

keyTerms.df: Boolean operators are used to construct compound conditions using and, or, and not.
keyTerms.eg: Boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
keyTerms.mi: Boolean operators only invert a single condition to determine the final outcome.
keyTerms.cx: Boolean operators not inverts a single condition; they build compound conditions using and, or, not.

scenario.su: A program checks if a user's age is over eighteen to grant access to a restricted area. The program must handle the case where the age is below the threshold by displaying an error message instead.
scenario.ma: Compare the logic for checking age 17 and age 20 against the requirement that an if statement runs its body only when the condition is true.

mc.q: Distinguish between the behavior of an if statement and an else clause regarding code execution flow.
op: The if statement runs its body when the condition is false.
The else clause runs its body when the condition is true.
The if statement skips its body when the condition is false.
The else clause runs its body when the condition is false.
mc.ex: An if statement skips its body when the condition is false, while the else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.

mc.q: Determine the result of a compound condition using boolean operators when checking if a user is an administrator or a moderator.
op: The condition returns True if both parts are false.
The condition returns True if either part is true.
The condition returns True only if both parts are true.
The condition returns True if the 'not' operator is used.
mc.ex: The condition returns True if either part is true, which is the behavior of the or operator.

lessonInput.title: DC circuits
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules. Claim 1: Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage. Claim 2: Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

claims: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

anchors.quote: direct-current circuits
series and parallel resistors
Kirchhoff's rules

facts: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

keyTerms.df: A DC circuit is a conducting path distinguished by steady current, sources, components, and conservation rules.
keyTerms.eg: Use the term DC circuit while comparing series components that share the same current with parallel branches that share the same voltage.
keyTerms.mi: A DC circuit has component voltages and currents that oppose conservation rules.
keyTerms.cx: Its component voltages and currents obey conservation rules along the conducting path.

keyTerms.df: Series components are circuit components distinguished by sharing the same current.
keyTerms.eg: Two series components in a DC circuit carry the same current.
keyTerms.mi: Series components are identified by sharing the same voltage.
keyTerms.cx: Shared current characterizes series components, while shared voltage characterizes parallel branches.

keyTerms.df: The junction rule is a Kirchhoff rule that expresses charge conservation.
keyTerms.eg: Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule express charge and energy conservation, respectively.
keyTerms.mi: The junction rule expresses energy conservation rather than charge conservation.
keyTerms.cx: Charge conservation corresponds to the junction rule; energy conservation corresponds to the loop rule.

scenario.su: Students must label a conducting path as a DC circuit and distinguish its series components from its parallel branches before a deadline. The steady-current notation, component current comparison, and branch voltage comparison must support one defensible classification despite the time constraint.
scenario.ma: steady-current path diagram, component current comparison, branch voltage comparison

mc.q: A circuit notation shows equal current through series components and equal voltage across parallel branches; which comparison correctly distinguishes the two observed component relations?
op: Series and parallel components share voltage
Series share current; parallel branches share voltage
Series and parallel branches share current
Series share voltage; parallel branches share current
mc.ex: Series components share the same current, whereas parallel branches share the same voltage. The reversed comparison incorrectly exchanges these two relations.

mc.q: A student compares junction notation tied to charge conservation with loop notation tied to energy conservation; which labels fit the records before the workshop deadline?
op: Junction and loop: charge conservation
Junction and loop: energy conservation
Junction: charge conservation; loop: energy conservation
Junction: energy conservation; loop: charge conservation
mc.ex: The junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation. Assigning energy to the junction and charge to the loop reverses the supported labels.

facts: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

keyTerms.df: A conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
keyTerms.eg: A circuit where a battery and a resistor are connected in a single path.
keyTerms.mi: A DC circuit only involves components that have constant voltage and current.
keyTerms.cx: A DC circuit involves sources and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.

keyTerms.df: Components connected in series share the same current flowing through them.
keyTerms.eg: Two resistors connected end-to-end in a single wire.
keyTerms.mi: In series circuits, the voltage across each component is identical.
keyTerms.cx: In series circuits, the current is the same, but the voltage across each component is not necessarily identical.

keyTerms.df: Branches connected in parallel share the same voltage across them.
keyTerms.eg: Two light bulbs connected across the same power source.

keyTerms.df: An electric field is a description of electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
keyTerms.eg: For points in space with different field-line density, use the density to compare relative field strength.
keyTerms.mi: The electric field points opposite the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Its direction agrees with the positive test charge's acceleration direction, rather than opposing it.

keyTerms.df: A positive test charge is the charge for which electric force per unit charge describes the electric field.
keyTerms.eg: The charge's acceleration direction identifies the direction of the electric field at a point in space.
keyTerms.mi: Field-line density gives the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Acceleration direction establishes field direction; density instead indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: Field-line density is the field-line property that indicates relative field strength.
keyTerms.eg: Comparing density at two points in space provides a comparison of relative field strength.

keyTerms.cx: The stated relation runs from the density of field lines to comparative strength, not in reverse.

scenario.su: A student must label two electric-field descriptions before a deadline, using a direction record and a field-line-density comparison. One description records where a positive test charge would accelerate, while the other compares denser and less dense field lines, so each label must follow the relevant relation.
scenario.ma: positive-test-charge acceleration direction record, denser-versus-less-dense field-line comparison, electric-force-per-unit-positive-test-charge passage

mc.q: At one point in space, a record gives electric force per unit positive test charge and an arrow gives the positive test charge's acceleration direction; what distinction is supported?
op: Field describes acceleration; direction follows force per charge
Field describes force per charge; direction follows acceleration
Field describes force per charge; direction omitted
Direction describes force per charge; field follows acceleration
mc.ex: The electric field describes electric force per unit positive test charge, while its direction follows the positive test charge's acceleration direction. Swapping those relations incorrectly makes acceleration describe the field itself.

mc.q: Two field-line displays differ in density, with the first visibly denser than the second; under a deadline, which comparison should the student record from that observation?
op: Second has greater relative field strength
First has greater relative field strength
Second describes force per positive charge
First has the positive charge direction
mc.ex: Field-line density indicates relative field strength, so the denser first display supports greater relative strength. Assigning greater strength to the less dense second display reverses the supplied relation.

mc.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the electric field from the electric force?
op: The electric field is the total force acting on a charge.
The electric field is the electric force per unit positive test charge.
The electric field is the direction a charge would accelerate.
The electric field is the total force exerted by surrounding charges.
mc.ex: The electric field is the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space, while the electric force is the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.

mc.q: A circuit has two points, A and B, where the electric field is measured. Point A shows a field-line density of 5, and Point B shows a field-line density of 10. What is the relationship between these two points?
op: Point A has a stronger electric field than Point B.
Point B has a stronger electric field than Point A.
Point A has a weaker electric field than Point B.
The field-line density is the same at both points.
mc.ex: Field-line density indicates relative field strength, so Point B has a stronger electric field than Point A.
